item.title: Hip & Pelvis — Deep Transverse Friction
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Hip & Pelvis and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: hip mobility, pelvic/SI-region symptoms, gait and functional loading.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Supine, prone or side-lying with the pelvis well supported.
Use a comfortable hip position and avoid forcing painful end range.
therapistPosition: Stand close to the pelvis/hip and use a belt when appropriate and trained.
stabilization: Stabilize pelvis when targeting the hip; stabilize the trunk/leg according to the pelvic technique.
contact: Use broad contact over proximal femur, pelvis or target soft tissue; avoid excessive pressure over groin neurovascular structures.
Identify a specific symptomatic tendon, ligament or muscle structure rather than rubbing a broad area.
Move transversely across the target tissue while minimizing sliding over the skin.
forceDirection: Use localized transverse loading that remains tolerable and does not provoke escalating pain.
dosage: Use short, symptom-guided bouts; progressive loading remains the main rehabilitation strategy for most tendinopathies.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Hip & Pelvis: hip mobility, pelvic/SI-region symptoms, gait and functional loading.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Screen fracture, severe OA irritability, postoperative restrictions, acute inflammatory pathology and red-flag pelvic symptoms.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Hip & Pelvis assessment → correct regional setup → Deep Transverse Friction → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Gluteal Tendon — Deep Transverse Friction
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Selected adjunct for localized lateral-hip tendon symptoms after careful differentiation from bursal and referred pain.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Side-lying with the treated hip uppermost and supported so compression is minimized.
subTechniques.contact: Use a precise contact over the clinically identified tendon region near the greater trochanter while avoiding direct aggressive pressure on the bony prominence.
subTechniques.direction: Apply small transverse movement across the tendon fibers.
subTechniques.dosage: Short tolerable bouts only; follow with progressive hip-abductor loading.
subTechniques.reassess: Single-leg stance, step-down and lateral-hip pain response.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Compression sensitivity is common in gluteal tendinopathy, so more pressure is not better.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid highly irritable lateral-hip pain where compression itself is strongly provocative.

subTechniques.name: Proximal Hamstring Tendon — Deep Transverse Friction
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Selected adjunct for localized proximal-hamstring tendon pain when symptoms are clearly tendon-related.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Prone or side-lying with the hip positioned comfortably and the tendon region accessible.
subTechniques.contact: Precise transverse contact over the tendon region near the ischial tuberosity while respecting patient comfort and privacy.
subTechniques.direction: Small transverse strokes across the tendon fibers.
subTechniques.dosage: Brief tolerable bouts followed by progressive hamstring loading.
subTechniques.reassess: Pain with sitting, resisted knee flexion/hip extension and functional loading.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Avoid prolonged compressive treatment at the proximal hamstring in a compression-sensitive tendinopathy.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Do not use if symptoms suggest acute avulsion or significant tear.
